title: How I got 100+ distinct weapons in one consistent art style, using AI-written Blender scripts instead of generators
author: The4modes
selftext:
I've found that generative AI art has a consistency problem: you mostly have to accept whatever it gives you. I had a lot of requirements that didn't fit that way of working, so I tried something else.

I'm making Brightest Blight, an Active Time Battle RPG in Godot, set in a grimy steampunk city where the night is a curse. It renders at 640×360 with a PS1-ish look, so a hero is about 70 px tall in battle. From the start, the whole idea was that gear should be unique and fun to collect.

The game now has 107 unique weapon models across 8 types: knives, sabres, rifles, gauntlets, flasks, lanterns, books and totems. I couldn't have made that many alone. I put a lot of effort into keeping one consistent art style that still feels like my game while using AI.

**What the AI does, and what it doesn't**

No image or 3D generators. Every model is a Python script run in Blender, written with Claude Code. My job is direction and review. The AI writes and fixes the scripts.

**Why it stays consistent**

* A shared kit. Every weapon is built from the same helpers (lofted grips, rings, rivets, plates) and one shared palette (worn walnut, gun metal, worn brass, copper, soot). A new weapon can't drift into another style, because it's built from the same parts and colours.
* A brief before any geometry. For each line of weapons I write a short brief: who owned it, what it's made of, and its one signature part (a hook, a drum, a bell). That part has to set the silhouette apart from other weapons of its type, not just the colour.
* Tiers and families as rules. Shop tiers go from worn to clean to fine as you level. Rare weapons come in four families, one per effect, each with its own colour and shape language: warm and traditional, soft green and round, deep blue and hooked, white-violet and sharp. Each has one faint glowing part and no aura. Rules like that make 100 weapons feel designed, not random.
* Readability over detail. Everything has to read at about 50 px, so the scripts favour chunky, rounded, oversized shapes. Detail only gets in if it can be seen from the battle camera.

**The checks that made it work**

* Every weapon gets preview renders: four angles, a black silhouette, and a render at game size.
* An automated clipping check runs the weapon on every hero who can wield it, through every animation, and lists anything that cuts through the body. Nothing gets shown to me until it's clear. Before this existed, renders kept hiding problems the check found.
* Then I look at it in the actual game, held in battle and stowed in town.

**What I learned**

* Scripts beat generated assets for consistency. A model is just numbers, so "make the blade 10 % longer" or "move it 2 cm off the coat" is a one-line change, and the model can be rebuilt any time.
* The AI is fast at variations. The taste, the briefs and the "no, that doesn't read" are still my job, and that's the part that keeps the style together.
* Writing down the mistakes as rules (no parts a few mm apart, or they flicker) stopped them from coming back which in turn made the creating process for game art quicker and quicker over time. The first few weapons could take a few hours of back and forth, now I can build all 8 weapons of different types with one coherent style in one go, usually needing only small fixes.

There's a free web demo on itch: [https://kingkrusbar.itch.io/brightest-blight](https://kingkrusbar.itch.io/brightest-blight) . I'm happy to share more about the pipeline. Is anyone else building art this way, through code instead of generators? What's worked for you?
